facts.statement: Albertonectes vanderveldei was described in 2012 from a skeleton found near Lethbridge, Alberta, in 2007.
facts.quote: The only known species is A. vanderveldei, described in 2012 from an almost complete postcranial skeleton discovered in 2007 near Lethbridge, in the province of Alberta, Canada.

facts.statement: The holotype was found accidentally by an excavator working for Korite International Ltd. during ammolite mining.
facts.quote: It was discovered unexpectedly by an excavator during ammolite mining carried out by the company Korite International Ltd.

facts.statement: Evidence of scavenging is preserved on the left coracoid, which bears grooves made by the shark Squalicorax.
facts.quote: The skeleton also preserves two teeth coming from the lamniform shark Squalicorax, the few traces of grooves present on the left coracoid indicating that the specimen would have been scavenged after its death.

facts.statement: Albertonectes lived in North America during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 73.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Albertonectes (meaning 'Alberta swimmer') is an extinct genus of large plesiosaurs that lived in North America during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period, at around 73.5 million years ago.

facts.statement: Albertonectes is the longest known elasmosaurid, with a maximum estimated length of 12.1 meters.
facts.quote: With a maximum length estimated at 12.1 m, Albertonectes is the longest known elasmosaurid.

facts.statement: Albertonectes holds the record for the greatest number of cervical vertebrae in any vertebrate, with 76.
facts.quote: It is also the vertebrate with the greatest number of cervical vertebrae identified to date, 76, ahead of its close relative Elasmosaurus.

facts.statement: The species name vanderveldei honors Rene Vandervelde, the founder of the mining company that found the fossil.
facts.quote: The specific name is named in honor of Rene Vandervelde, the founder of the Korite International, the gem-mining company that discovered the holotype.

facts.statement: Grooves on the left coracoid indicate the animal was scavenged by the shark Squalicorax after death.
facts.quote: The skeleton also preserves two teeth coming from the lamniform shark Squalicorax, the few traces of grooves present on the left coracoid indicating that the specimen would have been scavenged after its death.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen preserves 97 visible gastroliths (stomach stones).
facts.quote: The single known specimen of Albertonectes preserves gastroliths, 97 of which are exposed and visible.

facts.statement: The largest gastrolith found in the specimen weighed an estimated 1.13 kilograms.
facts.quote: The largest of the visible gastroliths weighed an estimated 1.13 kg.

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize that plesiosaurs specifically selected hard chert stones for their gastroliths due to durability.
facts.quote: It is hypothesized that chert stones were specifically sought out by plesiosaurs as gastroliths for their hardness and durability.

facts.statement: A 2024 study estimated Albertonectes' total body mass at around 4.8 metric tons.
facts.quote: In 2024, Henderson estimated its total body length up to 12.1 m and its total body mass around 4.8 MT.

facts.statement: A 2026 study provided a lower body mass estimate of 3.1 metric tons for an individual of the same length.
facts.quote: In 2026, Zhao estimated a lower body mass estimate of 3.1 MT for an individual of same body length.

facts.statement: The holotype is identified as a mature individual based on fused neural spines and partial fusion of the femur head.
facts.quote: Albertonectes is known from a mature individual, as suggested by the fused neural spines and most cervical ribs to their centra, and by the only partial connection between the trochanter and the capitulum (head) of the femur, seen in TMP 2007.011.0001.

facts.statement: In 2016, Rodrigo A. Otero established the subfamily Styxosaurinae to include Albertonectes and three other genera.
facts.quote: In 2016, Chilean paleontologist Rodrigo A. Otero established the subfamily Styxosaurinae to include four genera: Terminonatator, Styxosaurus, Albertonectes, and Elasmosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2020, the subfamily Styxosaurinae was formally synonymized with Elasmosaurinae.
facts.quote: In 2020, O’Gorman formally synonymized the Styxosaurinae with the Elasmosaurinae based on the inclusion of Elasmosaurus within the clade, and also provided a list of diagnostic features defining it.

facts.statement: The original authors noted that assigning Albertonectes to Elasmosauridae was problematic without a skull, as skulls provide key diagnostic features.
facts.quote: In their original 2012 description, Kubo and colleagues argued that assigning Albertonectes to the Elasmosauridae would be problematic in the absence of cranial material, as the skull provides key diagnostic features for newly described species.

facts.statement: The genus Albertonectes was described by Kubo and colleagues in 2012.
